# Developer Documentation

## Setting up the environment from scratch

### Prerequisites

-   Debian 12 (Bookworm)
-   Docker Engine + Docker Compose plugin installed
-   Git

### Add-ons

-   Visual Studio Code

### Configuration files needed before first run

The files containing sensitive data have to be added to the folder before launching the program with `make`:

-   `srcs/.env` — Env file contains the data to set up users and environment, define what type of role the user has and what the domain and database are called. 
-   `secrets/*.txt` — The folder will contain the passwords to access database and WordPress services, divided in the following files: db\_password.txt, db\_root\_password.txt, wp\_admin\_password.txt, wp\_user\_password.txt

Alternatively, the files can be created from scratch, it is however preferred to use the precompiled ones from the Host machine.

## Building and launching with Makefile / Docker Compose

```bash
make          # setup + build + avvio
make up       # come sopra
make down     # ferma e rimuove i container
make stop     # ferma senza rimuovere
make start    # riavvia container fermati
make restart  # down + up
make re       # fclean + all (ricostruzione completa da zero)
```

\[Spiega la logica interna: il Makefile chiama `docker compose -f srcs/docker-compose.yml`, quindi ogni comando è un wrapper\]

## Managing containers and volumes

### Useful commands

```bash
docker ps -a                    # returns a list of containers - active or inactive
docker logs <container_name>    # to check a specific container's logs
docker exec -it <name> bash     # to access a container
docker compose -f srcs/docker-compose.yml build --no-cache <service>  # rebuild forzato
```

### Volumes

\[Spiega dove sono i named volumes, come sono mappati su /home/giomastr/data, come ispezionarli\]

```bash
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect srcs_db_data
```

## Where project data is stored and how it persists

All important data is stored within two volumes that are saved on the VM’s drive, one dedicated to the database only, the other one stores necessary information for WordPress and Nginx containers.

-   `/home/giomastr/data/db` → MariaDB’s data (persistiti tra riavvii tramite named volume)
-   `/home/giomastr/data/wp` → WordPress files

Storing the data in volumes located outside the containers prevents the loss of necessary files and ensures their persistence, both in case of accidental or voluntary deletion of the containers.

Spiega il meccanismo di inizializzazione “once-only”: lo script [init.sh](http://init.sh) di ciascun servizio usa un marker (`.init_done` per MariaDB, il file `wp-config.php` per WordPress) per capire se deve inizializzare da zero o riprendere dati esistenti\]

## Architecture overview

The following diagram shows how the project’s flow is organised:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Three containers are build within the Virtual Machine, running on the most recent safe Linux distribution, Debian 12 (Bookworm). Being located on the same network, they can easily communicate between each other, without needing to dedicate a specific port for it. However, to be able to go online and reach the internet, it becomes necessary to specify that the connection will happen through port 443, NGINX container. 

\[Breve descrizione o rimando al diagramma del PDF: NGINX (443, TLS) → WordPress/php-fpm (9000, FastCGI) → MariaDB (3306) — tutti sulla rete `inception`\]
